The motion misnames the duty. A builder is not answerable for the harm as such but for whether they did what the position of builder requires towards the people who rely on the system. Roles carry duties after the fact as well as before. The relationship between builder and user does not end at the release, so a careful builder whose system harmed someone still owes them acknowledgement, an explanation, and help in making it right.

Humaneness is shown in how one responds to those one's work has affected. A builder who points only to the audit has misunderstood the relationship; one who meets the injured, explains and repairs is being what a builder should be.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that the Confucian measures the builder's duty from inside the role, when the people harmed were never asked what the builders owed them in the first place. That is a real gap in letting roles define duties: the people on the other end of a role may never have agreed to its terms. The answer is that a role's duties include listening to those it serves, and a builder who never asked has not met them. Builders ruled by penalties learn to escape blame, while builders who keep their role with a sense of shame learn to avoid the failure itself.

One is to blame for failing what one's role requires, not for the size of what went wrong, though the role still requires an account and repair. What you owe attaches to a position, not to the world at large. A builder owes the people their system touches care in making it, honesty about its limits, and an answer when it fails. A builder who did all of that has done what the position requires.

A Utilitarian will object that talk of what the role requires is beside the point, because blame exists to change future behaviour and should be assigned wherever it prevents the most harm. Blame used only as a lever stops tracking what anyone did, and people who cannot see why they are blamed stop trusting the roles that hold them together. The role tells you what to change; blaming the careful does not. Builders ruled by penalties learn to escape blame, while builders who keep their role with a sense of shame learn to avoid the failure itself.

Neither proportional blame nor walking away is what the role asks. The careful builder owes the injured an account and a share in repairing things, because that is part of the role too. Getting names right matters. To call a careful builder culpable in proportion to the harm is to use blame for something that is not fault, and once the word means that, it no longer distinguishes the builders who cut corners from those who did not.
